## Findings by module

### grid-down-food-1

- **confirmed** (ch-001.txt): Register with the local council Environmental Health Team at least 28 days before starting food operations; tell the council about significant changes and re-register as new owner of a bought business.
- **confirmed** (ch-002.txt): Two-stage clean: disinfectants only work on surfaces already cleaned of grease and dirt; follow dilution and contact time; disinfectants and sanitisers should meet BS EN 1276 or BS EN 13697. Matches the course callout to wipe dirt off before sanitising.
- **confirmed** (ch-002.txt): Fridges set at 5 C or below so chilled food is kept at 8 C or below, a legal requirement in England, Wales and Northern Ireland and recommended in Scotland; check at least once a day, probe between packs.
- **refined** (ch-001.txt): Personal hygiene before work: tell your manager about vomiting or diarrhoea and do not work with food; cover cuts with a brightly coloured waterproof dressing; wash hands after raw meat, eggs, unwashed vegetables, bins, phones and money.
- **refined** (ch-002.txt): Cloths: FSA says use disposable cloths where possible, one task each; re-usable cloths washed on a 90 C hot cycle, or washed then disinfected by boiling water or a suitable disinfectant; FSA states bleach is not a suitable disinfectant for cloths. Course l3 gives CDC bleach ratios for surfaces after flooding; show that the FSA business pack does not endorse bleach for cloths.
- **refined** (ch-002.txt): Business hand hygiene: hand rubs and gels (BS EN 1500) are an additional precaution and never a replacement for handwashing with warm running water, liquid soap and disposable towels; gloves are not an alternative to handwashing. Course l3 lets households use sanitiser when the tap is off (FSA household advice); the business lens must say a food business cannot run on sanitiser alone, so a water outage stops production.
- **refined** (ch-003.txt): Reheating means cooking again, not warming: reheat to a safe centre temperature, only once, stir microwaved food and test several places for cold spots; never put food into hot holding without reheating properly first.
- **contradicted** (ch-003.txt): Course l2 temperature table lists UK FSA hot holding as Not stated. The FSA SFBB pack says hot food must be kept at 63 C or above (with certain exceptions), and displayed hot food may come out of hot holding for up to two hours once only, then reheated, chilled to 8 C or below, or thrown away. Trust the FSA pack; fix the table cell to 63 C or above.
- **contradicted** (ch-004.txt): Course l2 temperature table lists UK FSA freezer as Not stated. The SFBB Prove it method says frozen food should be kept at -18 C or below, and calls hot holding at or above 63 C a legal requirement. Fix the UK FSA freezer cell to -18 C or below.
- **extended** (ch-001.txt): Written HACCP-based procedures are a legal requirement and it is an offence not to have them; SFBB safe methods must be completed before trading, with a diary filled in every day (opening and closing checks, anything that went wrong) and a 4-weekly review.
- **extended** (ch-001.txt): A temperature probe is the best way to show cooking, reheating, hot holding and chilling are safe (Prove it safe method). Inspection gives a Food Hygiene Rating 0 to 5; display is compulsory in Wales and NI, encouraged in England.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): Fitness to work: staff with diarrhoea or vomiting report it and stay home, and do not return until 48 hours symptom-free, because people can still carry harmful bacteria for 48 hours after symptoms stop.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): Separating: store raw meat, poultry, fish and eggs below ready-to-eat food, unwashed fruit and veg above raw meat; prepare ready-to-eat before raw where possible; colour-coded boards; never use the same slicer, mincer or vacuum packer for raw and ready-to-eat; do not wash raw meat or poultry (it splashes bacteria).
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): Physical and chemical contamination: store cleaning chemicals apart and labelled, use cleaning products suitable for food-contact surfaces per manufacturer instructions, no-glass rule, reject deliveries with foreign objects.
- **extended** (ch-003.txt): FSA safe time and temperature combinations for cooking: 60 C for 45 minutes, 65 C for 10 minutes, 70 C for 2 minutes, 75 C for 30 seconds, 80 C for 6 seconds. Course gives only 70 C for 2 minutes; the set shows time and temperature trade off.
- **extended** (ch-003.txt): Preparing produce: peel or trim outer parts, wash by rubbing vigorously in a bowl of clean water, cleanest first; clean then disinfect boards after soil-covered vegetables. Ready-to-eat food prepared on a surface or knife used for raw meat is thrown away.
- **extended** (ch-004.txt): Daily opening checks include fridges and freezers working, staff fit for work, hot running water at all sinks and hand basins, probe working, allergen information accurate; closing checks include throwing away food on its use-by date and recording Prove it checks. The daily diary is signed by the person responsible.
- **note** (ch-002.txt): Pest control: reject deliveries with gnawed packaging or insects; throw away food touched by pests; never let bait or sprays touch food or surfaces. Useful for grid-down storage where pests find stock.
- **note** (ch-003.txt): Checking doneness: probe the thickest part of the leg on whole birds, the largest piece of meat in stews and curries, and several places in large batches; juices clear, no pink. Eggs lightly cooked only if pasteurised or British Lion. Shellfish labels kept 60 days (legal). Acrylamide: cook starchy foods to golden yellow, deep-fry below 175 C.

### grid-down-food-cap

- **extended** (ch-001.txt): Legal requirement to record what food you bought, from whom, quantity, date and allergen information; keeping invoices and receipts usually covers it. Belongs in the capstone business plan (records).
- **extended** (ch-003.txt): Deliveries: keep food hot or cold until collected and during delivery to the customer's home, covered, ideally in an insulated bag or box. Supports the capstone dispatch rule.
- **extended** (ch-004.txt): Complaints (food poisoning symptoms, allergic reaction, foreign object): take seriously, check the diary, Prove it records, staff illness and similar complaints, consider removing the same batch from sale and telling the supplier, then change methods and retrain. Supplier records (what, from whom, quantity, date) are a legal requirement for traceability; check suppliers are registered.
- **extended** (ch-004.txt): Product withdrawal and recall: stop using or selling at once, label and remove affected batches, check whether the product went into food already made and frozen (ask the local authority), tell customers who may not eat it straight away, and report your own unsafe product to the local authority and the FSA. A frozen-meal business needs this in its continuity plan because stock sits in customers' freezers.
- **note** (ch-004.txt): The 4-weekly review flags any problem that recurred three or more times and asks whether probes were calibrated in the last 4 weeks; a contacts list (environmental health, electrician, plumber, pest control) fits the freezer-failure plan.

### grid-down-food-5

- **confirmed** (ch-004.txt): Phone or online orders: allergen information must be available before the order is placed and at delivery; meals for allergy customers must be clearly identifiable on delivery. Matches the course distance-selling rule.
- **refined** (ch-002.txt): 14 allergens list detail: tree nuts named (almonds, hazelnuts, walnuts, pecan, Brazil, pistachio, cashew, macadamia); cereals containing gluten include oats; sulphur dioxide when added above 10 mg/kg. Allergens cannot be removed or destroyed by cooking; if a mistake is made, start the dish from scratch rather than removing the ingredient.
- **refined** (ch-004.txt): Stock checks on delivery and in store: throw away punctured vacuum packs, swollen or blown packs and badly dented cans; check tops and seals; serving food past its use-by date is against the law; label frozen food with the date it was frozen; when decanting, record name, ingredients and date; first in, first out. Course l4 says examine dented commercial cans; the FSA business standard is stricter (badly dented cans thrown away).
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): Precautionary labels: if an ingredient label says may contain an allergen, tell the customer and ask if they still wish to order. Takeaway orders: keep an allergy customer's food separate, labelled and well covered in transport. Relevant to dispatch of frozen meals.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): Covering and storing: use containers designed for food; never re-use foil, cling film or freezer bags; do not store food in opened tins; avoid re-using single-use food packaging, as chemicals can transfer.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): Shelf life: high-risk ready-to-eat foods kept a maximum of 3 days in total (day of cooking or opening plus 2) unless there is evidence for longer. Once defrosted, a food's shelf life depends on the days left before expiry when it was frozen, so freezing pauses the date and does not reset it.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): Chilling hot food before freezing: avoid cooking large batches in advance; divide into small portions, cut joints, cover pans and stand them in cold water or use ice, stir, spread rice on a tray, or use a blast chiller; test methods once with a probe at intervals. If not chilled safely, re-cook or throw away. Freeze hot food as soon as it is properly chilled, in small portions in containers or freezer bags.
- **extended** (ch-003.txt): Processes outside the pack, including vacuum packing, sous vide, low-temperature cooking, fermenting, smoking and curing, must be shown to be safe, with advice from the local council Environmental Health Team. A frozen-meal business that vacuum packs needs this extra check.
- **extended** (ch-004.txt): Prepacked for direct sale (PPDS) food has needed the name and full ingredients list with allergens emphasised since October 2021. Free-from claims require an allergen-free environment; precautionary may-contain labels only after a full risk assessment shows a high cross-contamination risk. Update allergen information whenever a recipe or supplier product changes.
- **note** (ch-002.txt): Suspected anaphylaxis: do not move the person, ring 999 for an ambulance, say anaphylaxis, send someone to meet it, help them use their adrenaline pen.

### grid-down-food-2

- **refined** (ch-002.txt): The 4-hour rule in business: chilled food may be out of chilled storage for up to four hours, once only; under four hours it can go back at 8 C or below, over four hours it is thrown away. Label the time it came out.
- **refined** (ch-002.txt): Defrosting: ideally in the fridge; else in a container under cold running water (raw meat only in a sealed container), microwave defrost, or room temperature for the shortest time per manufacturer. Check for ice crystals with a skewer, joints flexible on birds; cook piping hot.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): Cleaning a fridge: move food to another fridge or cool box first so nothing sits at room temperature; empty fridges are the time to clean.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): FSA business freezer-failure actions: food still hard and icy goes to another freezer at once; food starting to soften or leak liquid continues defrosting by a safe method; fully defrosted food (soft and warm) is cooked if appropriate until piping hot, then used or chilled or frozen straight away, else thrown away; food that must stay frozen, such as ice cream, cannot be refrozen once it starts to defrost. Fits the freezer-failure log in l5 better than household estimates alone.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): If a fridge breaks down and you cannot move the food or do not know how long it was broken, contact the local council Environmental Health Team; food needing refrigeration kept unchilled for more than four hours is thrown away.
- **extended** (ch-003.txt): Ready-to-eat food: keep at most 3 days in total (day of cooking or opening plus 2) unless there is evidence for longer; cooked rice only 1 day once prepared. Gives a business-standard limit to set beside the household power-cut tables.
- **extended** (ch-004.txt): Checking a probe thermometer: in iced water it should read -1 to 1 C, in boiling water 99 to 101 C; outside that range replace or recalibrate; check about monthly if no maker guidance. Infra-red thermometers read surface temperature only and cannot check the centre of cooked or cooling food. Clean and disinfect the probe before and after each use.

### grid-down-food-4

- **contradicted** (ch-003.txt): Module 4 l1 callout says eating uncooked pasta or dried beans is CMO advice. The FSA pack says dried pulses such as beans contain natural toxins destroyed only by proper soaking and cooking per the packet, while tinned pulses are already cooked. The CMO list names beans among tinned foods; the callout's word dried is the error. Trust the FSA on dried pulses: rewrite the callout so ready-to-eat means tinned beans, and dried beans need soaking and cooking.
- **extended** (ch-003.txt): Foods needing extra care: cooked rice can carry spores that survive cooking and reheating and make toxins if left at room temperature, so keep it hot or chill it fast (spread on a clean tray, or rinse with drinking-quality water); dried pulses such as beans contain natural toxins destroyed only by proper soaking and cooking per the packet, while tinned pulses are already cooked. Both matter for grid-down cooking from dry stores.

### grid-down-food-3

- **refined** (ch-002.txt, ch-004.txt): Module 3 l5 says the FSA documents read set no rule for trading in a water outage. SFBB: handwashing needs warm running water and liquid soap, gels never replace it, and hot running water at all sinks and hand basins is a daily opening check. So the stop rule rests on FSA text, though the pack still names no outage rule as such.
